FAQ
Hedera ETF flows — common questions
Where does Hedera ETF flow data come from?
Which Hedera ETFs are tracked?
How far back does the Hedera ETF flow history go?

Hedera ETF flows show how much money moves into and out of U.S. spot Hedera exchange-traded funds each trading day. No market-data aggregator publishes this series, so the numbers on this page are computed from the issuers' own disclosures.

Inside the Hedera ETF market

The U.S. spot Hedera ETF market is a single-fund market: Canary HBR (0.95%, Nasdaq, listed October 2025). That makes the read unusually clean — every dollar of HBAR ETF demand passes through one product, so the daily flow is the demand, with no issuer-to-issuer rotation muddying the signal.

Hedera was one of the first altcoins after XRP to get a U.S. spot ETF, and it remains a single-issuer market. At 0.95% it is also among the priciest funds on this site — a reminder that first mover and cheapest are rarely the same product.

A creation means an authorised participant delivered cash or HBAR and received new fund shares: money entering the fund. A redemption is the reverse. Summed over time, these creations and redemptions are the cumulative net flow — the clearest available measure of how much regulated capital sits behind Hedera.

What drives Hedera ETF inflows and outflows
HBAR price momentum: flows into small crypto ETFs are strongly trend-following, and creations cluster after multi-day rallies.
Fee competition: with sponsor fees on these products ranging from zero to 2.50%, assets migrate toward the cheaper wrapper once several funds list on the same asset.
Advisor platform access: a fund only starts collecting steady flow once wirehouses and RIA custodians clear it, which usually happens months after listing.
Basis and arbitrage: authorised participants create shares when the fund trades at a premium to NAV and redeem at a discount, so flow often follows the premium.
Seed and conversion events: the first creation of a fund can dwarf months of ordinary flow, which is why a single day can move the cumulative line more than a quarter of trading.
How to read the data on this page

The daily chart shows net flow in millions of dollars: green is a creation day, red a redemption day, and a flat line means no baskets changed hands. Weekends and U.S. market holidays are absent because ETFs do not create or redeem then.

The cumulative chart adds those days up from the first day of trading, so it answers a different question: not "what happened today" but "how much money has this asset attracted in total". The fund table underneath breaks the same numbers down by issuer, with assets under management and the sponsor fee each fund charges.

Flows are computed daily from primary sources, not copied from another tracker. For each fund we read shares outstanding and net asset value per share straight from the issuer and compute the flow as the change in share count multiplied by that day's NAV, shifted one business day — a creation settles into the share count the following day. Canary publishes net assets and NAV but not share count, so shares are derived by division and rounded to the 10,000-share creation basket; the reconstructed NAV is checked back against the published figure to the cent.
